utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, this is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from the judges? Judge Clark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I have a number of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you were telling us over the last few days that you had spent a considerable time in the camp in - its name has escaped me for a moment, the one just outside Mostar - the Heliodrom, and that during that period, that you went 20 or 30 times to Mr. Stela's base or to other bases in the town to carry out forced labour. On each occasion, when you left the Heliodrom, were you transported in the same way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were always transported in the same way, that is, there was this blue truck, a Dais truck, and the driver was Dinko, whose surname I don't know. The driver, Dinko, would only drive us when we had to perform work for Stela. Whenever we were taken to some other units, it would be a different driver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That's the very question I wanted to ask you. Do you know if this man Dinko was attached to Stela's unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was a member of Stela's unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you think, at this remove in time from when you were in the Heliodrom, that you might be able to describe this man, Dinko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I might. He was rather dark, of medium height, maybe 178, 180, with cropped hair, and slightly receding hair. He also drove another vehicle, a privately owned vehicle, a smaller vehicle, an Ascona, I believe, which used to belong to a Muslim woman. And that's what I know about this man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: What was his build and his age, as far as you could ascertain? Was he slightly built, heavily built, broadly built?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that he was slightly built, of medium height, and he was between 37 and 40 years of age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Arising out of that, is Dinko quite a common nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we -- that's what we called him. That's what everybody called him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Have you heard other people with the nickname Dinko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to describe a man whose name came up a great deal yesterday - you mentioned him very frequently in your evidence - and that was an Ernest Takac. Could you describe him for me, please, if you can?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, he was a very dark man, dark-skinned man, and he had a beard, straight hair. He was also somewhere between 37 and 40 years of age, of medium height, perhaps 1 metre 76, 1 metre 80, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And what about his build?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was of medium build. He wasn't a -- he was not a very heavy person. He weighed perhaps 80 or 85 kilos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did anybody that you would meet on a regular basis wear an earring with a cross, have you any recollection, in your dealings with soldiers when you were a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but the majority of them used to wear earrings in those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So it doesn't stand out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: If I change the subject completely now, do you remember that yesterday you were talking about wooden rifles that were given to you? And I believe that you said that the wooden rifles were made by a man who was a prisoner who had been a carpenter. How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that for some time already. When we were placed in the sports hall at the Heliodrom, whilst we were there, somebody talked about some rifles being made. But we laughed at it because we didn't know what they would be used for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You said that on the day on which you were given these rifles, you had seen him painting the stock of one of them. Is that the extent of your knowledge of his connection with the manufacture of these rifles, or fake rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, I saw one rifle being finished by him. He was working on the rifle butt. He was painting it black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And I believe that your evidence was that this is the only occasion that you have personal knowledge of the use of fake rifles.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: When you were in Mostar, East Mostar, after your escape in September, did you meet -- did you become aware of the presence of a BBC journalist and a camera team in East Mostar at exactly the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did you -- I think you told us that you told your story about your escape, your incarceration, your work as a prisoner, and then your escape to the person that you think may have been from the MUP, or whatever, that evening. Do you think that story about the rifles became widely disseminated in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this for sure. I spent only two days in Mostar after I had crossed over. And after those two days, I left Mostar, that is, to be more precise, I left Mostar sometime around the 21st, in the evening hours on foot over the hills.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You had a colleague who was, like you, slightly injured and who made it over to the east side. Can we take it that he, too, was interviewed as you were and made a statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm sure that my colleagues, if they are called here, will tell you that. I know what happened with me. I don't know what exactly happened with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, in relation to this fake rifle, did it have a strap or any attachment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a strap, a green strap, an original rifle strap. And on top of those rifles, there was a nail which was supposed to imitate the sights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did you use the strap, and would that explain how you managed to hold onto the rifle in such extraordinary circumstances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were ordered to sling those rifles around our necks, and I was holding the rifle in the position ready to fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, one thing that you were cross-examined about yesterday by Mr. Par, who had some difficulty with it - and I have to confess that I do, too - I thought you said that when you got over to the other side - and I'm not sure whether this meant over the confrontation line or over the Neretva River - I think you said that someone asked you to hand over your rifle, and I wanted to know what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got over to the other side -- when I said that I got over to the other side, I was referring to the separation line and the building. Once we got to the building, we were afraid that they would kill us, and because of that fear, I took off my jacket, which means that I also had to take off the rifle. I gave the jacket to one of the soldiers there, I think the one that I jumped at when I -- when I got there, and I took the rifle and handed it over. Yesterday, I told you that, if necessary, I would put it in writing as to who has the rifle now and where it can be found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm not asking you -- I wouldn't ask you where the rifle is exactly. I know what you said about it. But when you said you handed over the rifle, did you actually hand over that imitation rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And then did you get it back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never gave it back to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, how do you know, then, what happened to it? I think there is a lot of confusion about this, and you're the only one who can sort this out at the moment. If you handed the rifle over to the soldier, the Armija soldier, at the confrontation line, with your jacket, how did you get the rifle back again in order to give it to somebody who put it in a museum? I'm not asking you for names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had handed over the jacket, and I had taken the rifle back and handed it over to another man. And I tried to locate the rifle. I searched for it. I wanted to have it back. Believe me, I would like to have it back, and I hope that I would be able to get hold of it one day, because it is a kind of memento, a precious memento for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm not sure you've quite cleared that up, but possibly the Prosecution can do it for me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of judge's questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Only one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see that wooden rifle in the museum?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Are you sure that it was your rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were not so sure, I wouldn't try to get it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have a question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, you told us that you learned about the wooden rifles at the Heliodrom and that the issue was discussed at the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How many were you in the sports hall at the time you discussed it and laughed about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many we were. We were one next to each other. There were quite a few of us, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In that sports hall, was the issue discussed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- not much at that time. Maybe later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the time when you laughed, when you heard about the fact that someone was manufacturing those rifles.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS OO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a very small group of people, four or five people perhaps, but I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Witness, for helping us by giving your evidence. We might invite you back to the Hague when we have that rifle and your statement if necessity requires. We are looking forward to your cooperation in the future. When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to thank the Court. As I have already told you, I have been eagerly awaiting for this moment. I am here for justice and nothing else. As to what it means, it means a lot for my people and my country. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would like to tender P14.5. It was marked by myself -- by the witness. So that's the only document that I want to tender today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think there's any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It has been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence also has some exhibits to tender, the statement, so I should like to tender D1/36 and D1/37, the two statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vinko Martinovic's Defence team would like to tender D2/20, the map that was marked yesterday. While we are waiting for our next witness, with the Court's indulgence, I should just like to say a few sentences about yesterday's debate. I don't know whether we have finished the debate or not, the issue having to do with cumulative charging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Wait. Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have one objection to the witness statements. Now we have a decision by the Trial Chamber dated the 14th of November in respect of witness statements, prior witness statements by the witness. They cannot be accepted as such, and I object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You do not object to the admission of that map?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: No, no, no. As for the map, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This map has been admitted into the evidence. Madam Registrar will give each a proper number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecution's Exhibit P14.5 is now PP14.5/9. The Defence exhibit D2/20 is admitted as DD2/20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I need some Court's assistance, having heard what the Prosecutor has just stated, and we are, of course, following your decisions very closely. But we really are not quite clear as to the relevance of the 14th November decision for the purposes of the present exhibits. The Prosecutor has referred to this decision, but I'm not really sure as to what the Chamber's decision is relevant for the purposes of the present statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this Trial Chamber made a decision concerning the admission of the previous statements by the witness on the 14th of November which said that in the principle, all those previous statements are not admitted into the evidence. This is the principle. And you tendered that statement which is D1/36 and D1/37, which we'll give each an ID number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct, Your Honour. But you also stated that you will take into account the contents of the statements, and that is why I didn't fully understand the objection, because if that is, indeed, the purpose of the objection, I have to say that these are the statements on the basis of which the indictment was issued. And if the Defence is unable to check the veracity of the testimony by using those statements, then I really do not know what the Defence can use as a basis for their cross-examination. Those statements were given to the Office of the Prosecutor. I really do not understand how we will be able to establish the truth if the Prosecutor himself is objecting to the use of his own statements. If that was the purpose of the objection of the Prosecutor, then I -- then I'm really at a loss. I mean, I just wanted to clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, the approach to statements does cause a problem when we are coming from two different legal systems. The system which appears to have been adopted by the Tribunal is an adversarial system, which means that the evidence which the Court receives is the evidence that we hear from the witnesses. We don't get the statements, we don't read the statements, because frequently, a witness will make a statement that's much stronger than his evidence in court, and that's just the way it goes. It's what the witness says in court that matters. So therefore, you are given the statement, the Prosecution is given the statement, and the Prosecution has to use that statement as a guideline for the witness without actually leading him at very material points, and the Prosecution are not permitted generally to raise evidence that doesn't appear in the statements. In other words, you can't be taken by surprise, because you're not prepared for something that isn't in the statement. So you use the statement to cross-examine the witness, to put to him, if it happens, as has happened many times here, "How are you giving evidence in relation to A, B, and C, when you made two previous statements when you didn't mention it at all and it's only when you say you were interviewed by members of the OTP that you remembered to say something which we can consider very crucial?" And you have very properly, all your team, cross-examined witnesses on this basis, and that is right and correct. But that doesn't mean that you then hand the statement in to us as evidence. Do you see the difference? What we have to do is to rely on your cross-examination and the direct examination. Now, there will obviously be very limited circumstances - Mr. Meek will know about this - there will be very limited circumstances in which the statement will become an issue. And I think in relation to one of the German mercenaries, indeed, we even asked to see the original statements, because there was a direct denial of the contents of the original statement, and therefore, it was important for us to see what this person had said previously? Can he be believed? Is he believable? Do we compare his evidence with someone else? In those very limited circumstances, obviously, the statement should become an exhibit. But because you come from an investigative system where the Judge investigates and statements are extremely important and they become the basis of the evidence, you want us to see the statements. But in the system that we operate, we shouldn't see the statements. So it's very important to have a good cross-examination. And obviously, you used the statements as the basis for your cross-examination, in addition to what the person said in court. So for that reason, the Trial Chamber has been trying -- and it is difficult. I come from a common law system; it's very easy for me to accept that. Judge Diarra and Judge Liu come from a system that's identical to yours. And obviously we are all on a learning curve. There is no one system that dominates over the other. But I understand, we all understand, this problem about statements, and that's why the Court made a very clear ruling that the principle is that we do not see the witness statements and they don't become exhibits. And there will be exceptions. I hope I've clarified that for you. It's not intended to prevent you from cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour, but then I believe I have properly understood the issue, because when I tender a statement, it is because I would like the Court to read the statement and to realise how contradictory it is to the testimony, and it is only then that I tender that statement. I do not do it very often, and that is why I thought that in this case, it should be taken into account and that the statement should be given to Your Honours for their perusal because you haven't had an opportunity to read it. You will only have an opportunity to read it once it has been tendered. That was the purpose of my tendering the statement. But I do understand the issue, and thank you once again for your guidelines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, as I told you just now, we will give those previous statements an ID number, which means that we will read it if we found it has probative value. If we found in some very limited circumstances, if we found that there is a preponderance of evidence in this case, this Trial Chamber will make proprio motu decisions to admit those previous statements into evidence. But anyway, they will not automatically come into the evidence in this system. I hope you could understand. Before this Trial Chamber, the live testimony before the judges comes first, since [Realtime transcript read in error "we do know"] we do not know under what circumstances all those previous statements was made, since we don't have a live witness to tell us about all those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think after this discussion, we all understand what this is all about, and my intention was precisely to -- for this to be taken into account after the Trial Chamber has realised how different the statement is from the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, I understand you are going to continue with the conversation yesterday, and I don't believe that it is the right time for this kind of discussion at this moment. And we also believe that the Prosecutor has already answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your leave, I would like to follow up on yesterday's response by the Prosecutor and say a few words. Perhaps, this is not the right time to follow up on yesterday's discussion, but I personally believe it would be a very bad idea to leave certain business here unfinished and to deal with different versions, different understandings of one issue in the future. That's why I want to have certain things cleared up from the viewpoint of the Defence, because I cannot allow the Prosecution to introduce certain things without properly objecting to them. I want to clarify certain points specifically with regard to yesterday's testimony involving wooden rifles. Yesterday, we have heard two positions. But let's take the official position taken by Mr. Scott, namely, that there were several incidents involving wooden rifles. The reason for this discussion in the first place was the testimony of Witness Knudsen, and the question was whether this was the same incident or not. We have heard the explanation that it may be a different event altogether; however, I reviewed the transcript of Knudsen's testimony yesterday and the remarks of the Prosecutor in announcement of that testimony, and the Trial Chamber's instruction that everybody should make a summary of the relevant charges in the indictment which would be covered by that testimony. In the Prosecutor's announcement of Witness Knudsen, the Prosecutor said that he would be covering charges 2 to 8 from paragraph 41 of the indictment regarding four prisoners moving ahead of a tank and carrying wooden rifles. That is why I cannot accept that Witness Knudsen's testimony, since it is not identical to the testimony of this eyewitness or another eyewitness, that it should be qualified as a different event altogether. I believe that the Prosecutor has told us clearly what this testimony is about and that we have understood him properly. If he says, as he said yesterday, that the Defence has not understood the indictment, I should only respond that the indictment should be formulated in such a way as to be understood by the Defence. Therefore, if the Prosecutor says that a witness would be talking about different events to those mentioned in the indictment, then he should also give us the basic parameters of these events. What is the date of that incident, that other incident involving wooden rifles? Who are those other prisoners who carried wooden rifles? So that we can prepare our Defence adequately. So, if the Prosecutor continues to stand by his claim that there were several incidents involving wooden rifles, we insist that appropriate witnesses would be called to support that. If the Prosecutor does not wish to do so, then the Defence should be enabled to call such witnesses themselves and to question them about this. To conclude, I would like to say that for me, it is not just the issue of the incident with the wooden rifles. There are analogous incidents such as that involving Professors one, two, or three, and the issue of whether Takac and others mistreated prisoners in only one place or several places, et cetera. I would very much appreciate the Trial Chamber's assistance in clarifying all these dilemmas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I completely agree with the Defence team of Mr. Vinko Martinovic, and I would like to add that this witness today was not the only one with whom we have such a problem. We have already had a witness who was a direct participant in the events and from whom we have a deposition. And the issue arose of whether Romeo Blazevic was involved in one incident or several incidents. Our position is that there was only one. And unless the Prosecutor specifies the charges in the indictment, we are prepared to proceed on that basis. Similarly, when I asked about the film, the video film, and I asked to be told what is the direct link between my clients and that video. I would really like the Trial Chamber to make these issues clear and definitive so that we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: On a different issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Meek. Let us concentrate --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: One thing at a time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott. We are not going into a debate. We just want to have a kind of balanced transcript at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously it is a debate. Defence counsel have now gone on for some minutes on a number of issues. So it is obviously an issue, and the Prosecution has to be given an opportunity to respond. First off, Your Honour, there has been extensive discussion this morning about the statements. And before we leave that issue entirely - because the Prosecution have not yet responded to those issues - let me say this about the statements, because I think that there's a misunderstanding of the statements in a number of respects. In that regard, it has now gone past on the stage, but there was a significant error in the transcript. It should be corrected. Because, Mr. President, you said a few minutes that the Chamber does not know the circumstances of which statements are made. The "not" on page 13, line 18 was not picked up. It says the Chamber does know the circumstances the statements were made. I understand, Mr. President, you said, "Does not understand." That should be corrected, page 13, line 18. Mr. President, I think the time has come to put the statements in proper perspective. Many, many, if not most of the criticisms, if you will, of the use of the prior interview statements can properly be characterised mostly as criticisms of the investigators or the statements and not fair criticism or fair impeachment in many respects of the witness. These are not verbatim statements. They are not like a court transcript we take down word for word. We have an investigator in the field who is taking a statement. He may write some things down; he may not write other things down. He may write something down incorrectly. There may be typographical errors. He may state the wrong date. He may ask about certain things; he may not ask about other things. We may a have investigator, Mr. President, going into the field who has been -- who has just joined the OTP several weeks ago and knows very little about the case. He doesn't know -- and I'm not criticising either the Chamber, obviously, or the Defence, but we have to put these statement into proper perspective. He may not know to ask certain questions. He comes back, he brings a statement -- he or she brings a statement back to the OTP. Those are the statements we have to use. It's unfair to suggest or infer in all instances that the witness has been inconsistent or the witness didn't say something before that he is saying now. He very well may have said it, very well may have said it, and it wasn't written down. We can't know that because, as you just said, Your Honour, the Chamber don't know the circumstances under which the statements were made. And that's exactly why, as Judge Clark will know, in the common law system the statements are not evidence. We bring the witnesses in here, and the witnesses testify. But I think the time has come, with all respect, that the use and perspective on these statements has to be clarified. So to repeatedly put to a witness, "You didn't say that in your statement three years ago," they might -- they weren't asked. Maybe the investigator should be criticised. Maybe I should take the investigator aside and say, "Why didn't you ask these questions?" But it's not a fair criticism, necessarily - we don't know - of the witness, and I think that has to be clear. Secondly, turning completely to the issue of the indictment, Mr. President, I can only suggest -- and perhaps it's been sometime since counsel have read the indictment. If counsel and the Chamber would turn their attention to paragraphs 35 through 42 of the indictment, I think the answer is clear on the face of the amended indictment. And I do invite the Chamber, in all seriousness, to turn to those parts of the indictment, if not now, Mr. President. If you don't want to take the time now, I suggest the Chamber do so in the near future. Those paragraphs relate specifically, just as Defence counsel said a moment ago - I'll try to slow down a bit - relate specifically to counts 2 through 8. It says that right on the top of page 11. It then goes on to say, in paragraph 35: "Between about April 1993 and at least through January 1994, Naletilic, Martinovic, and their subordinates forced Bosnian Muslim detainees from various detention centres under the authority of the HVO to perform labour in military operations and to be used as human shields, on the Bulevar and Santiceva Streets," et cetera, et cetera. Paragraphs 36 and 37 go on to -- they talk about prisoners being killed on the confrontation line, prisoners being used for forced labour, prisoners being used for human shields. It then goes on to say specifically, in paragraph number 40: "Throughout" - I'm quoting - "Throughout this period, Vinko Martinovic as the commander of the sub-unit Mrmak or Vinko Skrobo, regularly" - regularly - "used detainees for forced labour in military operations and as human shields along the confrontation lines in the city of Mostar." Then paragraph 41 very specifically talks about one particular wooden rifle incident with four men walking in front of the tank. That is one very specific incident. But it has never been the Prosecution case, and it is not said in the indictment, that was the only incident. It says clearly in the indictment this was a continuing pattern and practice, and it's evidence. It then goes on to say in paragraph 42: "On the same day, and about the same time, approximately 15 prisoners and detainees were deployed as a human shields in another part of the Bulevar also under Martinovic's command." Now, Mr. President, Your Honours, the indictment is clear on this. I stated our position yesterday. I state our position again today. I do not change it. It is the same. The Defence has been on fair notice, both from the indictment and in the 65 ter witness summaries, which have raised these issues over a year ago, so this is simply not fair. There is no effort - as I've said before, and as I will say again - there is no effort to add new or additional charges. They are charged with what they are charged with, counts 2 through 8. Paragraph 41 specifically talks about one particular incident. Other parts of paragraphs 35 through 42 talk about -- clearly provide for other similar incidents. There is no confusion. There is no good-faith confusion about this issue. And that is the Prosecution's position, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krsnik, we have already said that we are not going into a debate. We have a witness waiting outside, and we have a very tight schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I beg you, for just one minute. Precisely as my colleague Mr. Par said, the Prosecution is always introducing something through the back door and saying something which is absolutely not the truth. It is not true, Your Honour, that statements were taken on the ground by investigators who don't know the first thing. We have statements which were given first to the AID, the secret Muslim police. Investigators have been on the ground since 1995, and we monitored the names of investigators who appear in our case. All of them are experienced men who have worked since 1995 up to this day, with the support of the secret Muslim police called AID, and I, of course, mean investigators of the OTP. And also, the Prosecution, Mr. Stringer, Mr. Poriouvaev, have talked to many witnesses personally. And the greatest misgiving of this Defence -- and the Defence has been treading on this ground very carefully and trying to point out to this Chamber that these witnesses have been guided by the magic hand of some secret police, and we have been trying to point this out very decently and treat them with kid gloves. So the claim of the Prosecution that these details are not important is absolutely not true. All these statements are very important. All of the witnesses have read their previous statements and said that they were complete and truthful. Mind you, truthful. We are now in front of the International War Crimes Tribunal, after all. Secondly, we have read this indictment, and we know it by heart. That is precisely why we are reacting this way, because we want a fair trial. Yes, the Prosecutor did say that the counts covered such and such, but it is still a crucial point whether Romeo Blazevic was in Siroki Brijeg once or several times. We have to clarify this before the Court and with the Prosecutor, because if he was there only once, then it is a totally different charge. It makes a lot of difference whether he was in Ljubuski once or 20 times. The same thing with this latest incident, because we know it was only one incident, and the Prosecution is trying to spread it across a period of time. I am sorry to have taken your time, but I had to say this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as for the previous statement, we believe that this Trial Chamber has made a ruling on the 14th of November, and we also made an oral explanation concerning the meaning of that ruling. So I hope in the future there is no debate on this issue. As for the second issue, we all believe that the Defence counsel have the full right to challenge every detail of the live testimony of any witness before this courtroom. It is also our desire to make sure whether certain person has been to a certain place once or twice or 20 times. We believe that is essential to the case and to the right of the accused. We also believe that the answer from the Prosecution has satisfied the questions put forward by Mr. Par on this issue. We have the views correctly recorded in the transcript. In the future time, when we evaluate all this evidence, we will take into full consideration of the views expressed today by both sides. Let us go on with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Bos will be handling the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any protective measures you are going to request for the next witness, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And we may need to make some technical adjustments because the next witness has asked for face/voice distortion and a pseudonym. So I think that the technical people need 10 minutes to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: He is from that area?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he is. And he is afraid for the security of his family if he would testify without protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections? I guess there's no objections. Your request is granted. We'll break for about 10 minutes. We'll resume at 10.35 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my client is not feeling well. He would like to leave the courtroom, but we can, of course, continue with our usual schedule. And I don't think he will be able to attend the hearing tomorrow. He has the flu, and I don't know how he's going to feel tomorrow. But of course, we can continue in his absence, both today and tomorrow if he should not feel well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much for your cooperation. We are also worried about the health of your client. I hope he could have a good rest and speedy recovery. Mr. Naletilic, you may leave now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Maybe before we start, I'll mention the relevance to the indictment for this witness. It's relevant to background, paragraphs 7, 10, 11; superior authority, paragraphs 14 and 17; general allegations, paragraphs 20 and 21; count 1, paragraphs 26 to 28, paragraph 30, 34(a), 34(b), and 34(d); counts 2 to 8, paragraphs 35 to 38, paragraphs 40 to 42, and paragraph 44; count 21, paragraph 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Witness, the Trial Chamber has granted the protective measures you requested for. That means, first of all, the image of your face will be distorted and the voice will also be distorted and you will get a pseudonym. Now, in order to refer to your pseudonym, you're now going to be shown a sheet of paper which has your name on it and the name of your pseudonym. I would like you to confirm that this is indeed your name which is on that sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, where were you living before the war started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: I was living in Gacko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Bos, what's this gentleman's pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The pseudonym is Witness PP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In order to clarify this, so Witness, if I'm going to refer to you, I'll be referring to you as Witness PP, which is your pseudonym. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, is it correct that when the war with the Serbs started, that you and your family were expelled from Gacko and that you went to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And is it also correct that on the 16th of March, 1993, when you were living in Sarajevo, that you got wounded as a result of the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were you a soldier at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how -- what kind of injuries did you get on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: I was injured in my arms and in my eye. At that time, I was living in Hrasnica and there was no eye doctor there at that time, so I was transported to Konjic and from Konjic to Mostar, where I was hospitalised in Safet Mujic Hospital. I underwent treatment there until the 1st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I know you're not from Mostar, but do you know whether this hospital is located in West or in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: The hospital was in the area which was under the HVO control. I'm not -- I can't tell you exactly which side it was, but I think it was the right side of -- it was on the right bank of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that you -- so you got wounded on the 16th of March and that you remained in that hospital until the 1st of July; is that correct? We are talking about the year 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, while you were hospitalised in that period, did you notice that there were -- that the tensions arose between the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: No, nothing in particular. I mean, I didn't have much contact with other people, because I was in hospital on the 9th of May when these activities started at around 5.00 or 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But how did you know, then, that activities started on the 9th of May? How did you find that out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: The hospital was located at a critical location near Santiceva Street where most of the activity was taking place. We could hear detonations and there were talks about HVO units coming to the area. Actually, they did come to us. They checked on us. They were telling us that they had been attacked by the army and so on and so forth. So this is how we realised that the whole thing had started.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So are you saying that HVO soldiers did come into the hospital, and what would they do if they would enter the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: They came to the hospital on a regular basis. They were members of the Convicts Battalion. The reason for their regular visits to the hospital because -- was because they were members of this very special unit. They came to the hospital to mistreat us. They beat the patients. They treated us as extremists. And, for example, although those were seriously wounded patients, four of my colleagues had also had eye injuries, and with such injuries they were eventually taken to the camps. They called us terrorists and things like that, but we had nothing to do with that. We were merely patients at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you say that these members were -- that these HVO soldiers were members of the Convicts Battalion. How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: The Convicts Battalion -- we knew that they were members of the Convicts Battalion because they boasted about being members of that battalion and having Stela as their chief. They had special kinds of insignia which depicted a head of a dog, and they were named after Stela's dog, I think. Mrmak, something like that; that was the name of the dog. And they were members of this Convicts Battalion, Martinovic's battalion. I cannot recall his full name, but at any rate they were members of this Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you've testified how the soldiers treated the patients. How did they treat the doctors at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Badly, because the doctors who were there were rather fair and correct towards us, regardless of the ethnic background, and they protected us as best as they could. So that was the reason why they didn't treat them nicely. They verbally abused them as well, accusing them of keeping us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident with a doctor by the name of Amira Camdzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we do understand the need for leading questions in the introductory part of the testimony, but this is no longer an introductory part of the testimony, so the question how did they treat the doctors at the hospital was, I think, enough for the witness to provide his answer. However, if we should -- if the Prosecutor should go beyond that, I think that he would be leading the witness, which is inappropriate at this point in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bos, proceed another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall that there was a female eye doctor in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Yes. Her name was Amira Camdzic. The incident took place on the 1st of July when I was taken to the camp. She tried to protect five of us patients, but a member of the Convicts Battalion - I'm trying to remember his name, Dzemo Skobalj - he intervened. He actually assaulted this lady doctor. He pushed her away against the wall. He did so merely because she was trying to help her patients. That was the only reason why he pushed her away, why he attacked her so rudely, simply because she was trying to help her patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you find out what happened to her on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: I was then taken to the camp, but I managed to escape from the camp. And once when I got over to the area which was under the BH army control, I inquired about this lady doctor, and I was told that she had been expelled but was killed by a shell that exploded somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you've said that -- what happened to you on the 1st of July? Could you tell us again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: On the 1st of July, between 12.00 and 1.00 p.m., five of us were sitting in front of the hospital at the entrance to the hospital, and a group consisting of seven soldiers arrived. And one of those seven told us to move away. There were talks about the northern camp or -- in Bijelo Polje, some of their relatives may have been killed. Dzemo Skobalj was also amongst them. And he told us something like, "You stupid balija motherfuckers" -- I do apologise to the Court for using this language, but he verbally abused us and was accusing us. He started mistreating us, telling us that we were spies, snipers, how he had heard about us. And then they lined us up against a wall and tied our hands. I was trying to reason with Dzemo Skobalj because I knew him, but he wouldn't let me speak. And then, as I told you, this lady doctor, Amira Camdzic, tried to protect us, but he attacked her. And eventually we were taken away from there. I don't know the town of Mostar, but I think that we were taken to the students' campus there where there already quite a few women and children. That same evening, we were put on the buses and driven away. I don't know exactly what way we took, what route we took, but eventually we ended up at the Dretelj camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You've given us a long story, and I just wanted to clarify a few things. First of all, you told us that you knew Dzemo Skobalj -- that you knew him from before. How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Dzemo and I come from the same town. We went to school together. We knew each other from school. And when the war started, I found myself at the Igman Mount together with Dzemo. He had come to Igman together with the HOS. There was a HOS unit deployed there, and that is where I found him and made contact with him. But later on, he was transferred or he went to Mostar and became a member of the Convicts Battalion there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What is his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: He's a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Why do you think he became a member of the Convicts Battalion, if he was a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, that calls for pure speculation. I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, can you skip this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, I'll skip this question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, so you were taken to a collection centre in Mostar, and then that you were taken then to Dretelj. How many of you were taken to Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: As far as my bus is concerned, there may have been about a hundred people there. I cannot be more specific. Hundred approximately, where I was. Though, there were other people coming from elsewhere. I was put in one of the tin hangars, in a metal hangar at the Dretelj camp. But we didn't quite understand at the time what was happening, and so we were not -- I wasn't paying much attention to who else was coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: This group of a hundred people, were these women and children as well or just men, and were these people civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: There were only men on those buses. Whether they were soldiers or not, I don't know, but I know that they had been rounded up from their homes. I think they were civilians, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us what the conditions in the Dretelj camp were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: The conditions in the Dretelj camp were horrible, and I'm telling you this from my personal experience. I was put up in one of the tin hangars where there were some five or six hundred people there. The conditions were terrible. We had to relieve ourselves inside the hangar. There were very -- there were many elderly and sick people there, people who were dying because we hadn't received any water for about three or four days. The month of July, can you imagine what it means? The area of Capljina is very hot in that period of the year. People were being taken out of the hangar, beaten up, killed outside. They would open fire inside the hangar. People got wounded. Their wounds festered because no one could dress their wounds. It was terrible. But I didn't stay much longer at the Dretelj. I was then transferred to the Heliodrom, which was somewhat better.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just one question on what you just said. You said that people were taken out and killed outside. Did you ever witness a killing yourself when you were at the Dretelj camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: A man was taken out of the hangar on one occasion. He was stripped of his clothes, and they made him lie down on the concrete floor, on the concrete asphalt actually, which burnt his skin. Because it was very hot and he was made to lie down on the asphalt. And he was beaten up there. All kinds of things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I think we can break now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, how long did you stay in Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: About 19 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And when -- where were you taken next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: To the Heliodrom in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you were taken from Dretelj to the Heliodrom? With how many prisoners were you taken there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Many, because they had come to the hangar where I was. They said that Mostar people should be separated and taken out. So I was included into that group of Mostar men. And the same happened in other hangars. I saw a file of vehicles, cars, trucks. I don't know exactly how many, but about seven buses, I think, and I was in one of them. There were more trucks in that column. I can't say precisely how many came to Dretelj -- sorry, to Heliodrom from Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Heliodrom, where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: I arrived at the Heliodrom together with that group, which was together with me on the bus, and we were put in a gym. The gym was packed. There were five or six hundred people inside. That's where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was this gym -- was this one big space, or were there separate rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: There were two big halls under one roof, but it was two separate halls. I was in one of them. The other hall was the same, but it was also packed, so there were about five or six hundred people, maybe even more. It's just my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Whilst you were at the Heliodrom, were you ever taken out to perform labour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: I was taken out to work on a regular basis. We went to Buna and Santiceva Street, to Sovici, Doljani, Risovac, and Rastani. Although I'm not familiar with the town of Mostar and I'm not able to place the location exactly, but I know it was in the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned several places. Could you tell the Court what kind of work did you have to do, the various type of tasks you had to perform.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Specifically, I'll tell you what kind of jobs I did. I picked cherries at Buna. I think it's called the cherry field, Visnja, a plantation where I spent several days. For two days, I dug trenches in Mostar. I worked carrying stuff out of private apartments and houses and loading them onto trucks. In Rastani, I dug trenches again, built bunkers. In Sovici, Doljani, Risovac, the same thing all over again, before I arrived at Santiceva Street near the health centre. That was my last day, the last day I did labour before I escaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go into detail on some of the tasks that you had to perform, but before I do, could you please describe what the regular procedure was when you were taken out for labour? How did that work? Would people come and pick you up? Could you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: They came to pick us up every morning. I'll tell you specifically about places around Mostar where we went. Dinko or Vinko Martinovic came to collect us. I don't know. Sometimes it was Dinko, sometimes it was Vinko. There were two men. He came with two soldiers or two policemen from the Convicts Battalion every morning, and they took us away every morning. They made up groups of people which were sent to various places, which did different jobs. Sometimes we carried stuff out of houses and apartments. Sometimes we filled sacks with sand. Sometimes we took bunkers apart. Sometimes it all happened in the line of fire and people got killed. People were asked to destroy trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you there? You've said in the morning there was this person who you referred to as either Dinko or Vinko Martinovic. He would come and collect prisoners. Were you always collected by this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Martinovic came as a driver to pick us up every day. As regards Stela, he came every day. But the people who accompanied us were not the same every day. They changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you always work with the same prisoners? If a group would be collected, would it always be the same prisoners, or would that vary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: No, it was not always the same men. They changed. Sometimes people were wounded and couldn't go out any longer. Sometimes they were killed. Sometimes people were sick and were not able to go out to work. Anyway, it was not always the same group, so to speak. They changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would a person just come and say, "Today I'm going to pick this, this, and this person," or would they have a list, or how did that work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Somebody would come with a list; and if somebody on the list was missing or unavailable, then he would just point his finger at anyone in the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, so you've stated that you would usually be picked up by this person which you either refer to as Vinko or Dinko Martinovic. Is that what you said? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Sometimes it was Dinko; sometimes it was Vinko. It was the same person, but he introduced himself on some occasions as Vinko and on other occasions as Dinko. But it's the same person. Martinovic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In what kind of vehicle would he come and collect you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: On a Dais truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you remember the colour of that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: A blue truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you give us a description of this man which is called either Dinko or Vinko.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: He was about 180, 185 centimetres tall, well-built, brownish hair with a parting in his hair. He was about 80 kilos, in my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And do you know for whom this Dinko or Vinko worked? Who was his superior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Stela.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: I know because he would say, whenever he came, "The boss ordered," or "Stela ordered," things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you ever see Stela yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did you ever see this Dinko or Vinko together with Stela?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When was it that you saw this Dinko or Vinko together with Stela? Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: I remember that they were together on the day when I escaped. He said that he had left a group behind somewhere at the entrance to Mostar, about 10 men. He was telling him where he had left whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sorry, if you say "He was telling him where he had left whom," who do you refer to as "he" and who is "him"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Vinko was reporting to Stela where he had left each group of men. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You've said that you were taken out in groups. How many prisoners would be in a group on average?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: When they were taking them out?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, when they were taken out of the gym. You said you were taken out in groups. How big was a group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Well, a bus full, about 30 people or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know how many groups on a normal day would be taken out of the gym?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: I can't say precisely. Sometimes I know that the gym would be only half full; sometimes it would be empty because everyone had gone out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, earlier in your statement, you said that you sometimes were taken to private houses to take out goods from private houses. How many times did you do this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Yes. On a couple of occasions, I did that kind of work. We took goods out of houses and loaded them onto trucks. They were then transported to Siroki Brijeg. Those were chest drawers, refrigerators, household appliances, things like that. We did that two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: These houses where you took out these goods, were these houses inhabited by people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Of course they were inhabited, but those people who lived in them had been expelled, driven out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And on those occasions that you were taken out to perform these tasks, who drove you? Was it always Dinko who -- on those occasions who took you from the gym, or don't you -- well, who took you from the gym? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have a problem here with the name of this person who took out men from the Heliodrom. Mr. Bos is perfectly aware of this. We also know that this problem had appeared in the earlier statement of this witness. We are all eagerly expecting to hear what this witness is going to say, which name he's going to mention, and Mr. Bos is now using both names in his questioning in order to end up using only one name. Since this is a controversial issue, I would like him to refrain from doing that. I don't think he's doing it on purpose, but I do wish to point it out as something unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, first, I believe that Mr. Bos will clear it up for us. And if not, secondly, you have the full opportunity to do your cross-examination concerning with those names, if you're not satisfied with the question put forward by Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection is to the leading question, leading the witness to only one name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Rephrase the question and try to make things clearer for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: On those occasions that you were taken to take out goods from private houses, who drove you from the Heliodrom to those places?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: The driver was this Dinko. I'll try to clarify it for the ladies and gentlemen. On some days, it was Vinko. On other days, it was Dinko, to us, because sometimes we would call out to him, "Hey, Vinko." He would curse our mothers and say, "I'm not Vinko. I'm Dinko." That's the problem, and you know it very well, gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what was his last name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You've mentioned a couple of places where you also performed labour, and one of them was Sovici Doljani. Do you recall when you were taken there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: It was in mid-August, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Who took you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: I don't know who took us there. All I know is we went there on a truck. We were picked up from the gym in the middle of the night, and we arrived at Sovici early in the morning. We had travelled all night before arriving there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What kind of work did you have to do there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Cleaning houses in Sovici. We dug trenches, chopped wood. We buried dead cattle because combat operations had taken place there a couple of days previously. There was a lot of dead cattle, and we buried it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know which HVO units were involved in the combat -- whether -- what kind of units were involved in the combat operations in Sovici Doljani? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: I can't tell you that very precisely. I wasn't there at the time of the combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, whilst you were working at confrontation line, did you ever see prisoners getting mistreated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you give me some examples of what you've seen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Well, one specific case happened on Santiceva Street. We were digging trenches shielded by sandbags, and one member of the Convicts Battalion walked up. He was drunk, and he threw a hand grenade, killing one man. Muharem Gudic was his name. There were other cases, but I'm describing one which I witnessed personally. And they called us names and verbally abused us. They were saying things like, "Balijas are kicking our asses and throwing hand grenades."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were you ever mistreated, physically mistreated, yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Yes. I got one beating at Dretelj. There were provocation, frequent provocations. Sometimes they would just hit you, slap you, verbally abuse you, and then beat you. That was the kind of thing that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were you ever taken out to bury bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: In Risovac, when I worked there, a cemetery was dug there, graves, that is. That's what we call them. It's a Muslim term. I dug a total of nine graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name where this was, because it didn't appear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Risovac, near Sovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you actually dug these graves, did you also see the bodies that were put in the grave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know at the time you were working there how many graves in total were dug?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: I know about nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: This cemetery, what kind of cemetery was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: It was not a cemetery. It was a field at Risovac, not a cemetery at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When was the last day of your detention at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: My last day of detention was the 19th September, 1993, when I made a run for it while acting as a human shield.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness PP, let's go into detail on that day. First of all, what time in the morning were you picked up from the Heliodrom and who picked you up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: It was 6.00 a.m. Vinko Martinovic came, or Dinko, to avoid confusion. He came to pick us up with two guards, escorts, as you wish, on a truck. They loaded 31 of us on a truck. Some 10 people did not go with us all the way. They were left just before the bridge to work on a house just before the entrance to Mostar. About 10 or 15 of us arrived at the Health Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. What happened when you arrived at the Health Centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: We were unloaded from the truck, and we were standing in that yard outside the Health Centre. They divided us into groups, and my group was given the job of cleaning rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How many members were in your group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Three or four of us in the group where I was, those of us who were cleaning the rifles, three or four men. There were several groups of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Please continue. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, interpreter's microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, maybe you can start again because the interpreters didn't catch the beginning of your question. Can you start again from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: From the time we arrived at the Health Centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, from the time that you were cleaning the rifles.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: So I was part of that group that was cleaning the weapons. Four men were taken to a cellar which was next to the building. I don't know what was going on inside, but at one point, I saw one of them being taken out. He appeared to have passed out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Could you ask the witness to slow down, please, if he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness PP, I think you heard the request of the Judge. If you could slow down in your story so that everyone can understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: So I saw them taking one of the young men out of the cellar. He appeared to have lost consciousness. I saw them trying to help him come to. Then a man by the name of Dado, whom they refer to as Dado, arrived. I remember that he was a very tall man, 190, 195. He had dark complexion and a beard, and he told me to follow him into the cellar. And I went to the cellar, and I saw Mr. Stela sitting at a desk which had a map on it. And he told me to sit down, and he said "If you behave properly, you will have everything. You will have all kinds of privileges. You will be able to go to third countries. No one will harm you in any way. However, you should behave yourself and do as we say. You have to be a good boy."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Again, the interpreters have difficulties in keeping up with you because you talk very fast. So again, I would ask you to talk a bit more slowly. While -- let me ask you a few questions on this. So you said you were taken to the basement and that you -- that you saw Stela behind --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: First of all, how did you know that this man was Stela?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Because I had seen him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And when had you seen him before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: I had seen him when coming to work, when he came to verbally abuse us, calling us names, balijas, cattle, things like that, when he came to visit us as we were digging or doing some other kind of work. Mostly in the morning when we were brought to work, he would show up. So I knew his face. I knew that this was Stela.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How many occasions had you seen Stela before that time you saw him behind the desk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: One or two -- two occasions. I remember two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And do you recall on those two occasions where you were actually working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: In that same area. Again, I'm really not familiar with the town of Mostar. He was usually in the area around Bulevar, and that was the location where I most frequently worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, so you came into the basement, you saw Stela behind the desk. Were there any other people in the basement at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: There was no one else in the cellar except for this very short man by the name of Dolma. When I entered the cellar, he was standing at the door. So I sat down, and, again, as I told you, he told me that if I -- if I behaved properly, if I'm a good boy, I would -- he would -- that I would be able to leave. And I said what I was supposed to do, and he said that I would go across the street; if there were any wounded persons there, that I should recover them, pull them out. And he said, "If everything is fine, if the work is done successfully, you will -- you will be okay." So they brought me a uniform, I put a uniform on and got out of the cellar. This person by the name of Dado gave me a backpack full of stones. He put it on my back. And Stela brought a bottle and -- an empty bottle and put it in my pocket, telling me that it was supposed to be my Motorola. Once again, Stela appeared with a cardboard box. He put it on a wall, and he said, "Give this cattle here two bandages each," so each of us was given two bandages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you again? When you were given this uniform, were you the only one given this uniform, or were there other prisoners who were also given this uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: The three other men had already been given uniforms. They were in the cellar as I was cleaning the rifle. When this young man fainted - I don't know exactly what happened to him - they came out of the cellar and I got in. So they were dressed in the same uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, and after you were taken out of the cellar, were you taken to that other group of prisoners who already had a uniform on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: It all happened in the same area, outside the building, the same yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, you testified that you were also given a rucksack and that Stela had put something in your jacket. What did he put in your jacket?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: A plastic bottle. He put it in my pocket, and he said, "The balijas will think it's a Motorola."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: A young man showed up. I don't know who he was. And he brought four wooden rifles. I was to be given one of them. Dado brought us to a passage between those two buildings, and he said, "You should cross over the street and you should cross that lane as well," because it was a two-lane street. "Wait for us at that building, at the corner of that building there." I remember two news-stands on the sidewalk near the street. I passed those news-stands, and I reached the other street. And Dado spoke again, and he said, "Not that building. The one on the left," and he again cursed me. I don't know what was happening exactly at that moment because the tank opened fire. I was getting lost. But I had managed to reach the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I know this must be difficult for you, but I think we will have to go a bit more slower through this evidence. First of all, what did they ask you to do? What was your assignment when you -- after you were given the rifle? What did they want you to do? I think you said --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Combat activities were supposed to start at any moment. The area of Cernica Mala - that was the name of the neighbourhood - was where we were supposed to cross over to the other side of the street so the members of the Convicts Battalion could also cross over. And in case of death or wounding, we were supposed to recover either the bodies of the wounded people from that spot. So we were supposed to reach that building. We took to the left of the street, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm going to stop you there. When you gave your statement to the investigators, is it correct that there was a sketch drawn of the area and the places where you were and where you were actually going? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I recall it quite well, although I was afraid. But I do remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in order to assist the story you're going to tell us now, I'm going to show you the sketch. And maybe with reference to the sketch, you can explain us exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the sketch I would like to mark is Exhibit P888. The Defence has already received a copy. I have copies for the Judges. And it has to be submitted under seal because the name of the witness is on the sketch, and I have put a redaction on one of them so we can put it on the ELMO. I have covered the name of the witness on the sketch so that we can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, before you, you see this sketch. Do you recognise this sketch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to explain - and try to do it as slowly as possible - what happened to you from the moment that you were given the wooden rifles and you were ordered to go out. And maybe you can use the pointer and the sketch to indicate where you actually went and what happened.
